# Holiday Shoppers Are Asking AI First, and Retailers Need to Be Ready

> **In short:** Salesforce projects AI will drive $75.8 billion in Cyber Week spending, up 13% from 2025. Almost 20% of shoppers now start with AI, but most still click "buy" themselves, and a few bad recommendations can lose them.

Picture this: you want a stand mixer for a relative, so you ask an AI assistant to find the lowest price, check the reviews, and warn you if it won't arrive in time for the holidays. Then you close the app and buy it yourself. According to Salesforce, that kind of shopping is becoming normal.

## Where shoppers start now

Salesforce says AI is expected to influence more than 1 in 5 holiday orders this season. Its survey of more than 2,500 shoppers in the U.S., U.K., Canada, and Australia found that almost 20% now treat AI as their first stop before heading to a store or website. Traffic from AI tools to online stores has also more than doubled compared with last year, according to the company.

The most common jobs people give their AI helpers are comparing prices, digging through reviews for sizing or technical details, and brainstorming gift ideas based on what they want. Salesforce also reports that 30% of shoppers who use AI say it often introduces them to brands they had never heard of.

## Why shoppers still check out themselves

Here is the twist. Shoppers trust these tools for advice, but they are not handing over their wallets. Salesforce reports that only 19% of people who use a personal AI agent (an assistant that acts on your behalf, like searching and comparing for you) have let it reach checkout. Of all shoppers surveyed, 73% say they are not comfortable giving an AI their payment details.

People who do let agents buy tend to set firm limits. Some keep a separate credit card just for agent purchases, which caps the damage if something goes wrong. Common worries include sharing purchase history, and accidental or unwanted charges.

## Why mistakes matter so much

Trust is easy to lose. Salesforce says most shoppers will stop using an AI assistant after just two or three mistakes, and 32% of them blame the AI when a recommendation goes wrong.

For retailers, the company says brands with their own shopping agents see bigger orders and more loyal customers. Salesforce's advice to them is to keep product details accurate, keep prices and stock current, and make sure their own agents can answer tough questions.

## What this means for you

- **In everyday life**: Use AI to compare options and read reviews, but keep your payment details to yourself until you have checked the final price and delivery date. Set a clear budget before you start.
- **For your business or work**: If you sell products online, check that your product descriptions, prices, and inventory are accurate. AI helpers will read them, and so will your customers.
- **If you're just getting started**: Ask an AI assistant to list the pros and cons of two products you are considering. Then check the details on the store's own page before you buy.
- **If you already use it**: Ask your assistant to flag shipping cutoff dates and return policies, not just prices. Then confirm those details on the retailer's site, because cheap prices mean little if the gift arrives late.

## Wrap-up

AI is becoming a regular part of holiday shopping, from first ideas to price checks. Shoppers seem happy to let it advise them, but most still want to press the final button. For everyday shoppers, that is a sensible rule to keep. Today, try using an AI assistant to research one gift idea, then verify the price, delivery date, and return policy directly on the store's website.
